narrator.name: Ala Shaabana
narrator.role: Co-founder, Bittensor and the Opentensor Foundation; co-founder, Crucible Labs
narrator.affiliation: Opentensor Foundation (2019 to 2026), Crucible Labs (2024 onward)
narrator.one_line: The academic half of the founding pair: a McMaster applied-computing PhD and ex-VMware distributed-systems engineer who co-built Bittensor with Jacob Steeves from 2019, ran the foundation's operations, left for Crucible Labs, and explains the network in engineering and institutional terms rather than in Steeves's biological ones.

statements.quote: As with other commodities, markets could help us efficiently produce machine intelligence. We propose a market where intelligence is priced by other intelligence systems peer-to-peer across the internet.
statements.context: Opening of the abstract of the Bittensor whitepaper, published under the pseudonym Yuma Rao and credited to Steeves and Shaabana as co-authors.

source.title: Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market

statements.quote: Standalone engineers cannot directly monetize their work and what results is centralization where a small set of large corporations control access to the best artificial intelligence.
statements.context: Introduction of the whitepaper, stating the problem the market is meant to solve; authorship is pseudonymous so the words are credited to the founding pair rather than to Shaabana alone.

source.title: Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market

statements.quote: A new commodity needs a new type of market. This paper suggests a framework in which machine intelligence is measured by other intelligence systems.
statements.context: Whitepaper introduction, naming intelligence as a commodity and the network as the market for it.

source.title: Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market

statements.quote: Bitcoin is designed in such a way that this digital commodity is very easy to to validate, right? Hashes are immediate to validate and everybody can agree
statements.context: On the Towards Data Science podcast with Jacob Steeves, explaining to host Jeremie Harris why validating intelligence is harder than validating Bitcoin hashes.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: Any TAO on the system has actually been mined fairly. So it's actually contributed to the general knowledge of the whole system. We didn't kind of do any kind of initial coin offering.
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, answering how the token was distributed.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: every 12 seconds or so there is a new block generated. And with that block, there's one TAO that is awarded to the highest performers
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, describing the block reward mechanism to a machine learning audience.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: One of the big inefficiencies of AI is...retraining stuff over and over, right? The other kind of side that is also inefficient is the idea of contribution. Today...if I want to contribute to, let's say, an open AI or some massive GPT model...I really kind of have to be either part of the Googles and the Facebooks of the world.
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, explaining what is broken in how AI is currently produced.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: We're an API. And since we are effectively a gigantic, decentralized mixture of experts, what happens is at the mid-tensor layer, any model that you create is going to have...it's really a way to pick experts.
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, describing what Bittensor is in machine learning terms; the auto transcript renders Bittensor as mid-tensor.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: At BitTensor, the idea is that you as a human have no input over what models you're talking to. It's your own model that's picking and choosing who to talk to, who is best for it. So we kind of remove this human bias part of it.
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, on why peer ranking by models replaces human benchmark curation.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: Information itself on the network also compounds. Right. You don't need to relearn things anymore because you're speaking to other models and might have already learned something that your model doesn't know yet.
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, on the benefit a researcher gets from plugging a model into the network.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: I find it a little bit more terrifying that a single company, like I don't want to mention, would own AGI compared to all of us owning a piece of it
statements.context: Towards Data Science podcast, asked about the risks of powerful AI concentrated in a few labs.

source.title: 123. Ala Shaabana and Jacob Steeves - AI on the blockchain (it actually might just make sense)

statements.quote: Because BitTensor is essentially one large mixture of experts model, you can have it interface with these different environments
statements.context: Bittensor Hub AI Sessions episode 1 on Discord, discussing how models on the network could be pointed at tools; the auto transcript attributes this to Shaabana but speaker labels in that transcript are unreliable.

source.title: AI Sessions With Bittensor | Episode 1 (Sept 19, 2022)

statements.quote: And I think that the way that BitTensor incentivizes intelligence is very much in that same vein. ... And to know that it's producing something that is incredibly valuable and incredibly productive to the betterment of mankind or humankind is fantastic.
statements.context: Bittensor Hub AI Sessions episode 1, closing remarks after a discussion of productive resources; the auto transcript attributes this to Shaabana but speaker labels are unreliable.

source.title: AI Sessions With Bittensor | Episode 1 (Sept 19, 2022)

statements.quote: Nakamoto is going to stay the same. We are going to be either launching on Kusama or Polkadot, depending on how this Finney soft launch goes.
statements.context: TGIFT Finney update recorded on the Bittensor Discord with Jacob Steeves, telling the community how the Finney launch would proceed.

source.title: Bittensor | TGIFT | Finney Update (01.10.23)

statements.quote: We will be winding down Nobunaga in the coming weeks. I will post up an announcement about it as we do it, but Nobunaga is becoming obsolete in the next couple weeks.
statements.context: Same TGIFT Finney update, announcing the retirement of the Nobunaga test network in the operator's voice.

source.title: Bittensor | TGIFT | Finney Update (01.10.23)

statements.context: TGIFT Spaces session 2, explaining why Finney launched as its own chain instead of a Polkadot parachain.

source.title: Bittensor Spaces: Session 2 | TGIFT | (March 9, 2023)

statements.quote: you don't have just one massive network or one massive monolith. Now you have small subnetworks...these subnetworks can actually take care of different aspects
statements.context: TGIFT Spaces session 2, introducing the subnet architecture that Finney enables to the community.

source.title: Bittensor Spaces: Session 2 | TGIFT | (March 9, 2023)

statements.quote: delegation will actually allow you to maybe hold a few TAO and then be able to earn on that TAO as you delegate to some bigger validator.
statements.context: TGIFT Spaces session 2, explaining delegated staking to small holders.

statements.quote: Due to their public nature, open source AI projects, such as Bittensor, often lead these discussions, influencing the standards around responsible AI.
statements.context: Built In op-ed written by Shaabana the week of the Biden AI executive order, making the case for open source AI.

source.title: 3 Reasons AI Should Be Open Source

statements.quote: Contrast what we've learned about open source AI in this article with the recent executive order, which states that every company training an AI model must report this model to the U.S. government and obtain approval.
statements.context: Built In op-ed, turning from the case for open source to the executive order as its foil.

source.title: 3 Reasons AI Should Be Open Source

statements.quote: Further, the executive order maintains a status quo in which only a few corporations can wield AI for their own purposes. Open source AI seeks to democratize and decentralize this power for the greater good.
statements.context: Closing lines of the Built In op-ed.

source.title: 3 Reasons AI Should Be Open Source

statements.quote: Bittensor's roadmap to dissolve its own foundation over time, completing the decentralized vision through demonstrable self-governance.
statements.context: Delphi Podcast with Tommy Shaughnessy recorded during the OpenAI board crisis; this wording is the show-notes summary of what Shaabana said about the foundation's role, not a transcript line.

source.title: Ala Shaabana: Beyond the OpenAI Silicon Valley Echo Chamber: Decentralizing AI with Bittensor

statements.quote: as Bittensor continues to scale, the community must further accelerate progress by expanding resources and capabilities, and most importantly, decentralizing away from the Opentensor Foundation and into the world
statements.context: Medium post announcing Crucible Labs as a validator working in parallel to the foundation; the page returned 403 and this wording comes from a search engine excerpt of it.

statements.context: Zoom interview with Forbes contributor Tor Constantino, describing subnets after dynamic TAO; the Forbes page returned 403 and the wording comes from a search engine excerpt of the article.

source.title: This Open-Source Company Is Quietly Working To Transform AI

statements.context: X post quoting Sami Kassab's line that four or five successful subnets could make Bittensor a generational success and that more than ten are approaching product-market fit; reached through the fxtwitter mirror of the post.

statements.quote: It's like if three people in the world owned all the libraries, teachers and computers, and everyone else needed permission to use them
statements.context: Interview with CoinDesk's Margaux Nijkerk for the Most Influential profile of Sam Altman, describing the concentration of AI power.

source.title: Most Influential: Sam Altman

statements.quote: We looked at projects like Folding@Home or SETI@Home. They were distributed, but they lacked proper incentives, and ultimately they failed. That's when it became clear that blockchain was the missing piece.
statements.context: Written Q&A with Jeremy Le Bescont for CoinShares' The Node, asked what drew him to blockchain.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: AI has a fundamental verification problem. Blockchains are very good at verification... you get a trustless, permissionless environment where work can be verified transparently. In many ways, AI verification is the use case blockchains have been waiting for.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked why AI and blockchain work well together.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: One way to think about it is as a brain. Another is as a city. Bittensor is made up of 'subnets', which you can think of as neighbourhoods or specialised regions. Each subnet solves a different problem — storage, inference, training, object generation, defect detection.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked whether it is correct to describe Bittensor as a brain.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: You also have researchers, including people from traditional Web2 AI labs, who are increasingly interested in decentralised training because it produces more resilient, generalist models.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked who is using Bittensor today.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: It all comes down to incentives. Without a token, everyone races to solve the same problem and earns nothing, which is exactly why earlier distributed compute projects failed. By aligning incentives properly, Bittensor gives everyone a fair opportunity to earn based on the value of their work.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked why a token is essential to the network.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: The OpenAI governance drama highlighted just how centralised AI power has become... At the same time, Bittensor is fully open-source, incentivising transparent AI development. And importantly, the ecosystem has reached a point where builders are moving faster than the core team.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked what is driving Bittensor's momentum.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: Decentralised AI changes this by letting you talk to many models at once, with validators selecting the best responses. Instead of one ChatGPT, you're speaking to a room of them. That brings resilience, nuance, and scale, and it opens the door to models with trillions of parameters.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked whether decentralised AI is a way past current LLM limits.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: I think Bittensor could become something like TCP/IP for AI. Most people don't think about TCP/IP, but it underpins the entire internet. I see Bittensor becoming that underlying layer, quietly powering AI development everywhere.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked how he sees Bittensor evolving.

source.title: Interview: Ala Shaabana, Bittensor

statements.quote: Very early. We were among the first to coin the term 'crypto AI', and now you're seeing massive valuations being raised for problems we're already solving. That tells you two things: the market is only starting to understand the value here, and the wave is coming.
statements.context: CoinShares Q&A, asked whether decentralised AI is still early.

foundation.mission.summary: A market that prices machine intelligence peer to peer so that anyone can contribute and be paid for it, and so that AI's power is democratised and decentralised rather than held by a few corporations.

foundation.vision.summary: Bittensor as the unnoticed underlying layer for AI, a TCP/IP, made of many specialised subnetworks rather than one monolith, with the foundation itself dissolving into the network over time.

foundation.values.summary: Fair launch with no ICO, open source, permissionless competition from anywhere, and removing human bias from who gets to contribute.

problem.cultural.summary: AI power is concentrated in a few hands, which he pictures as three people owning all the libraries and teachers and everyone else needing permission.

problem.market.summary: AI is verified badly and produced inefficiently: work is retrained over and over, contribution requires belonging to Google or Facebook, and earlier distributed projects like SETI@Home died for lack of incentives.

problem.institutional.summary: A single company owning AGI, or a regulator requiring approval for every model, locks in a status quo where only a few corporations wield AI.

opportunity.summary: AI verification is the use case blockchains were waiting for; the OpenAI governance drama, the arrival of subnet product-market fit, and a macro turn away from sovereign trust all favour open incentive networks.

audience.summary: Machine learning researchers and Web2 labs in the early years; small TAO holders through delegation; subnet founders and startup investors after dTAO, told to market as well as build.

positioning.category.summary: An intelligence market and a decentralised mixture of experts in 2022; a city of subnet neighbourhoods, TCP/IP for AI, and Bitcoin's mining side made programmable by 2026.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Models rank each other without human curation, many models answer at once, and each subnet is its own entity tied to TAO, unlike one monolithic model.

positioning.reason.summary: Incentives are the whole argument: blockchains verify, tokens align contributors, and what a subnet rewards is what its miners will optimise for.

positioning.against.summary: OpenAI and the closed labs, the Googles and Facebooks as gatekeepers of contribution, the Biden executive order's reporting regime, Polkadot as a home for the chain, and closed coding tools on price.

value.functional.summary: Earn TAO for useful work or by delegating, plug into compounding knowledge, get many models' answers at once, and draw on a large annual emissions subsidy.

value.emotional.summary: Relief from the fear of one company owning AGI, and pride in producing something valuable to humankind.

messaging.h1.summary: Open source AI decentralises power for the greater good; AI verification is the use case blockchains were waiting for; Bittensor is Bitcoin's mining made programmable and could be TCP/IP for AI.

messaging.proof.summary: Block rewards, a 100 million dollar a year emissions subsidy, subnets approaching product-market fit, Web2 researchers joining, a subnet five to seven times cheaper than Claude Code, and Bitcoin's hash rate as the proof that incentives marshal compute.

voice.summary: Operator's register: launch logistics, wind-downs, chain choices, and a Munger-style aphorism about miners; plain and institutional rather than prophetic.

relationship.summary: Co-founder and operator who ran launches from the foundation, then built Crucible Labs to pull the network away from the foundation, and by 2026 speaks as an ecosystem investor who says builders now move faster than the core team.

language.term.summary: Commodity and market from the whitepaper; mixture of experts and API in 2022; subnetworks in 2023; crypto AI as a term he claims to have coined; subnet tokens, subsidy, and subnets as startups after dTAO.

coinages.meaning: The category label for token-incentivised AI networks, which he says the founders were among the first to coin.
His March 2023 name for what became subnets: small purpose-specific networks replacing one monolith.
Bittensor described as Bitcoin's mining side made programmable on a new chain.
Emissions described as roughly 100 million dollars a year handed to builders.

genealogy.summary: The whitepaper voice, shared with Steeves, frames intelligence as a commodity that needs a new kind of market and names corporate concentration as the failure to fix [ala-shaabana-001] [ala-shaabana-002] [ala-shaabana-003].

To a machine learning audience he describes Bittensor as an API and a decentralised mixture of experts, stresses the fair launch and the block reward, and states the anti-monopoly case as fear of one company owning AGI [ala-shaabana-008] [ala-shaabana-005] [ala-shaabana-011]. By early 2023 he is the operator announcing launches and wind-downs [ala-shaabana-014] [ala-shaabana-015].
genealogy.shift: From market abstraction to engineering description and operational voice.

genealogy.summary: He explains the move to a solo chain and introduces subnetworks against the monolith, delegation for small holders, and the idea that anyone can build on top [ala-shaabana-016] [ala-shaabana-017] [ala-shaabana-018] [ala-shaabana-020].
genealogy.shift: Subnets enter his vocabulary; the frame becomes software architecture rather than one big model.

genealogy.summary: In the week of the OpenAI board crisis and the Biden executive order he argues for open source AI as a matter of who may wield the technology [ala-shaabana-023] [ala-shaabana-022], tells Delphi the foundation should dissolve over time [ala-shaabana-024], and in late 2024 leaves to start a validator that decentralises away from the foundation [ala-shaabana-025].
